title: API and boundaries
summary: Name client operations and the service boundary that owns each one.

parts.rule: Translate requirements into a small external contract: operations, identifiers, essential request and response fields, errors, and idempotency where writes may repeat. For each mutable entity or field, name one authoritative owner. A boundary may be a module inside one service; do not require a network hop merely to draw a clean ownership line.
parts.why: The API reveals what must happen synchronously for the caller and what can finish later. Ownership prevents two components from accepting conflicting updates to the same truth. If the design jumps directly to internal services and tables, it is hard to tell whether the client can perform the required workflow or who resolves concurrent writes.
parts.example: For a ride-hailing MVP, define POST /trips to request a ride, POST /trips/{tripId}/accept for a driver, POST /trips/{tripId}/complete, and GET /trips/{tripId}. POST /trips carries rider_id, pickup, destination, and an idempotency key; it returns trip 781 in REQUESTED state. Trip owns that state. Location owns current driver coordinates and may be queried during matching, but it cannot update Trip.status. When driver 9 calls accept with expected_version=3, Trip performs one conditional transition from REQUESTED version 3 to ACCEPTED version 4. A competing driver receives Conflict instead of creating two accepted drivers. Completion changes Trip first and emits durable billing work with trip_id and fare; Billing owns charge status and reports its result without directly rewriting the trip row. This gives every write one owner even if the MVP uses one deployable application and one database. Splitting Trip, Location, and Billing into separate services is a later deployment decision. Also name failures: a duplicate create returns the earlier trip for the same idempotency key, an unknown id returns NotFound, and an already accepted trip returns Conflict. These contracts make the subsequent read and write paths testable.
parts.use: Draft the API after scope and before the detailed component diagram. Use it to assign identifiers and write ownership, identify concurrency checks, and separate response-critical work from asynchronous side effects. Keep the first boundary set coarse enough that one request does not require a chain of tiny calls.
parts.refuse: Do not create ten network services for five operations or give two modules authority over one status field. Avoid undocumented side effects and chatty endpoints that expose internal table steps. Sharing storage in an MVP is acceptable, but sharing it must not become permission for every component to write every row.

body:
Rule. Translate requirements into a small external contract: operations, identifiers, essential request and response fields, errors, and idempotency where writes may repeat. For each mutable entity or field, name one authoritative owner. A boundary may be a module inside one service; do not require a network hop merely to draw a clean ownership line.

Why it matters. The API reveals what must happen synchronously for the caller and what can finish later. Ownership prevents two components from accepting conflicting updates to the same truth. If the design jumps directly to internal services and tables, it is hard to tell whether the client can perform the required workflow or who resolves concurrent writes.

Worked example. For a ride-hailing MVP, define POST /trips to request a ride, POST /trips/{tripId}/accept for a driver, POST /trips/{tripId}/complete, and GET /trips/{tripId}. POST /trips carries rider_id, pickup, destination, and an idempotency key; it returns trip 781 in REQUESTED state. Trip owns that state. Location owns current driver coordinates and may be queried during matching, but it cannot update Trip.status. When driver 9 calls accept with expected_version=3, Trip performs one conditional transition from REQUESTED version 3 to ACCEPTED version 4. A competing driver receives Conflict instead of creating two accepted drivers. Completion changes Trip first and emits durable billing work with trip_id and fare; Billing owns charge status and reports its result without directly rewriting the trip row. This gives every write one owner even if the MVP uses one deployable application and one database. Splitting Trip, Location, and Billing into separate services is a later deployment decision. Also name failures: a duplicate create returns the earlier trip for the same idempotency key, an unknown id returns NotFound, and an already accepted trip returns Conflict. These contracts make the subsequent read and write paths testable.

[[diagram:boundary]]

When to use. Draft the API after scope and before the detailed component diagram. Use it to assign identifiers and write ownership, identify concurrency checks, and separate response-critical work from asynchronous side effects. Keep the first boundary set coarse enough that one request does not require a chain of tiny calls.

When to refuse. Do not create ten network services for five operations or give two modules authority over one status field. Avoid undocumented side effects and chatty endpoints that expose internal table steps. Sharing storage in an MVP is acceptable, but sharing it must not become permission for every component to write every row.
